- Nike has announced its newest pinnacle racing shoe, the Apex
- It features a redesigned midsole with stacked Zoom Air units
- The new marathon racing model will be released on January 7
The super shoe frenzy just got even more intense: Nike recently announced the Apex, the brand’s latest elite marathon racer. The Apex won’t go on sale until January 7, 2027, but pros are already wearing it—and it’s already on the podium. Here’s what you need to know about this soon-to-be-released super shoe.
Specs
From a distance, the Apex follows the same general design as the Alphafly models before it: an airy mesh upper over a thick foam midsole with a carbon fiber plate and Zoom Air units in the forefoot. But the Apex has some major updates compared to its forebears. The most obvious: This shoe features four Zoom Air units, arranged in two sets stacked on top of each other, in the forefoot (the Alphafly 4 has only two such units). The ZoomX LT foam, a revised PEBA-based material also used in the Alphafly 4, returns in the Apex, but Nike tweaked the carbon fiber plate design to guide your foot forward onto the Zoom Air units for maximum responsiveness and propulsion. All that adds up to a shoe that weighs a feathery 5.9 ounces in men’s size 10.
The other big change? The Apex is a zero-drop shoe, measuring an even 40mm across at both the heel and forefoot. No other super shoe on the market has a zero-drop platform; even Altra, a brand famous for its zero-drop models, gave its top-tier racer a 4mm drop. Nike claims the flat footbed provides a more balanced ride and lets the brand pack more cushioning into the Apex without breaking the World Athletics 40mm stack height limit.
Super shoes aren’t designed for durability, but Nike definitely wants you to save the Apex for race day only. In the shoe’s official press release, the brand notes it’s designed “to serve runners for at least 100 kilometers.” That means you can expect to cover about 62 miles in these kicks before they start to wear out.
What It Means
As usual, Nike makes bold claims about its new design, but the stats for the Apex are particularly impressive. Nike reports the new shoe generates up to 40% more energy return than the Alphafly 3 (the brand didn’t offer a comparison with the Alphafly 4) and weighs 10% less in a men’s size 10. All that performance comes with an eye-watering price tag: This shoe will retail for $360 per pair.
Pros are already putting the Apex to work, and it has seen success—both the third place men’s and third place women’s finishers in the Chicago Marathon wore Apexes.
The rest of us will have to wait until January to try the Apex, but the Alphafly 4, now Nike’s No. 2 racing model, goes on sale on Oct. 29. Check out Jeff Dengate’s AF4 shakedown here, and bookmark Nike’s Apex page for more announcements on its pinnacle racer.

Do you want a permanent income stream from the stocks you own? It's easy to find stocks with high dividend yields. Unfortunately, most of them are mature, sometimes stagnant businesses with only enough growth to support slow, steady increases.
Why not dial up the difficulty to find a generous dividend that can still easily outpace inflation for years to come? Philip Morris International (PM +2.67%) yields 3.2% and has raised its dividend annually since it began trading in 2008.
Its most recent increase, a hefty 8.8% bump, is impressive and no fluke. Here's why investors can buy, hold, and look forward to increasingly generous dividends from this tobacco giant for the foreseeable future.
The legacy business still shines
At first glance, it's fair to wonder why one might invest in tobacco stocks. Smoking rates have been declining for decades in the United States. However, Philip Morris primarily operates outside the United States, selling Marlboro worldwide.
The smoking decline isn't as straightforward in international markets, where rapid population growth has helped buoy the number of smokers despite the actual smoking rate decreasing.
Whereas sister company Altria Group, which sells Marlboro in America, reported a 3.2% decrease in domestic cigarette volume in the third quarter of 2026, Philip Morris' volumes held flat. Pricing power enabled the company to boost its organic gross profit from combustibles by 7.4%. In other words, cigarettes remain a very viable business internationally.
The future is coming sooner rather than later
That hasn't stopped Philip Morris from pushing to shift its business toward reduced-risk products, such as oral nicotine salt pouches, electronic vapes, and heat-not-burn tobacco devices.
The products have accounted for a whopping 42% of Philip Morris' net revenue through nine months of 2026. That puts Philip Morris squarely in the driver's seat in this industrywide race to a future beyond cigarettes.
With both major business segments thriving, Philip Morris has a strong growth outlook. Analysts see the company growing earnings by an average of nearly 9% annually over the next three to five years, and I wouldn't be shocked to see that pace sustained longer due to the immense pricing power nicotine creates.

Hyperscalers need power, and a lot of it. Constellation Energy (CEG +1.56%) operates as one of the largest independent power producers and has been signing long-term deals with hyperscalers left and right as companies scramble to secure energy.
Over the past month, Constellation Energy secured two more long-term agreements, this time with Amazon (AMZN -3.90%) and Alphabet's (GOOG -12.87%)(GOOGL -13.10%) Google. The deals provide visibility into Constellation's future earnings while also helping fund power upgrades and expansions to meet future demand from data centers.
Here's what investors need to know about the deals and what they mean for Constellation Energy's stock over the next decade.
Constellation Energy's long-term deals with Amazon and Google add power capacity
On Sept. 30, Constellation Energy inked a 20-year power purchase agreement (PPA) with Amazon for 690 megawatts (MW) of power. As part of this deal, Amazon will help fund a 190-MW uprate at Constellation's Maryland nuclear power plant, Calvert Cliffs Clean Energy Center, with new capacity coming online between 2030 and 2032.
A week later, on Oct. 6, Constellation locked in another 20-year PPA with Google that would help bring 890 MW of new nuclear capacity online in the PJM Interconnection region. This agreement locks in long-term revenue for Constellation while enabling it to invest in nuclear equipment across its plants in Illinois, Pennsylvania, and New Jersey.
Long-term agreements de-risk Constellation Energy's business model
As an independent power producer (IPP), Constellation Energy owns power-generation assets, including the largest nuclear power fleet in the U.S., natural gas plants, and other renewables. Unlike regulated utilities, Constellation doesn't own the power lines or transmission network. As an IPP, it isn't subject to regulatory-set prices and sells electricity into the market at prevailing rates.

We’ve all been there: You head out for an easy run and settle into your usual pace, but after a mile or two, your breathing feels labored and you notice your heart rate climbing higher than normal. However, you’re still going at your usual pace on your usual route, so what gives?
If you judge the run by pace alone, you might see no reason to change anything. But those other signals suggest you’re paying a higher price than usual to hold that speed.
Of course, you probably already know that factors like heat, hills, fatigue, and stress can make your usual pace feel harder. But with so much advice about what to pay attention to during a run, it can be tough to know which signals to trust and how to use them to evaluate your effort.
And without a clear way to interpret those signals, you might inadvertently push too hard on an easy day or miss the intended effort during a speed workout. Repeat these mistakes, and over time, you can disrupt the balance between training and recovery, making it harder to build the fitness you need to race your best.
The solution: A system from ultramarathon runner and endurance coach Nick Farr, head coach and founder of P3 Fitness. Farr organizes running feedback into three categories—performance output, biological load, and subjective feedback—and uses them together to understand how a run is unfolding.
Here’s how to use Farr’s three-category system to make every run count, build fitness more consistently, and arrive on race day ready to perform your best.
Why Your Run Data Needs Context
“No single metric tells you the whole story [of a run],” Farr says. For example, your pace tells you how fast you ran. But, inherently, it can’t tell you how difficult that pace felt or how your body responded to that pace.
To get a fuller picture, Farr separates training feedback into three categories, each of which answers one of those three questions:
- Performance output: What work are you doing?
- Biological load: How is your body responding to that work?
- Subjective feedback: How does the effort feel?
Evaluating the answers to these questions in concert with one another helps Farr and his athletes understand whether a run matches its intended purpose. It also gives runners a way to recognize when environmental conditions, fatigue, or other factors might call for an adjustment.
Performance Output: Shows What You’re Doing
Performance output describes the work you produce during a run. Metrics like pace, speed, distance, time, elevation, cadence, stride length, and power fall into this category, Farr says.
These metrics help you track what you accomplish. They show how quickly you covered a route, how far you ran, or how much climbing you tackled. You can also compare output across runs to see how your performance changes over time.
But output alone offers an incomplete view of the effort. You might finish an easy run at your usual pace, even though heat, hills, or fatigue made it much harder than normal. If you focus only on the pace number, you could miss the signs that you pushed beyond the effort you intended.
Biological Load: Reveals How Your Body Responds to Effort
Biological load, which Farr also calls internal or physiological load, describes how your body responds to the work you’re doing. Numbers such as heart rate, breathing rate, oxygen consumption, and core temperature can all offer information about your body’s response to a certain pace, environment, or training block.

Adobe (ADBE -0.66%) stock hit its closing record of $688.37 on Nov. 19, 2021. Almost five years later, shares of the creative software company trade around $248 as I write this -- about 64% off that high. And at their June 25 closing low of $193.41, they were down about 72%, the stock's deepest drop since the dot-com crash.
Deep drops are nothing new to Adobe, though. Using daily closing prices since 1990 (adjusted for stock splits, with dividends left out), the stock had fallen at least 30% from a record close eight times before this slide. It then set a new record after every one.
But I don't think that history settles much, because the two slumps this one most resembles started with a problem today's Adobe doesn't have.
Image source: Getty Images.
The slow comebacks took around six years
Six of the eight drops came in the 1990s, and they were deep, running from about 31% to 66%. But they were also mostly short.
Five of the six went from one record close to the next in around 18 months or less. The longest, which bottomed in August 1998, took about 3.4 years.
The two drops after that were another story. After peaking on Nov. 6, 2000, Adobe stock lost around 80% by August 2002, and it didn't close at a new record until Nov. 16, 2006.
The next slump, from an Oct. 24, 2007, peak, cut the stock around 67% by March 2009. Its next record was on July 12, 2013, about 5.7 years after the 2007 high.
Both times, the climb from the bottom back to the old high took over four years by itself. Today's slump is almost five years old, and as of this writing, the stock would have to gain around 177% to get back to its record.
In 2002 and 2009, the business shrank first
In the first of those long slumps, Adobe's revenue shrank two straight years, from fiscal 2000's $1.27 billion to $1.16 billion by fiscal 2002. Net income fell around a third over the same stretch.
Then sales turned. Revenue climbed 11% in fiscal 2003 and accelerated to 29% growth in fiscal 2004, so investors who hung on could see the rebound in the numbers.
The 2008-2009 recession cut deeper. Fiscal 2009 revenue slid 18%, to around $2.9 billion.
Interestingly, the stock's 2013 record was in a year when revenue fell 8%. Adobe had stopped new releases of its Creative Suite software, which customers bought outright, to focus on Creative Cloud subscriptions, which spread out revenue over time. Investors pushed the stock to a record before the new model's sales caught up.
Is this time different?
In one big way, it is: Adobe's business never shrank this time. Management expects fiscal 2026 revenue of around $26.6 billion, about 69% above the $15.8 billion it pulled in during fiscal 2021 -- the year the stock peaked.
Adobe's revenue climbed 13% year over year in its fiscal third quarter of 2026 (the period ending Aug. 28, 2026), hitting a quarterly record of $6.76 billion. Its non-GAAP (adjusted) earnings per share climbed even faster, up 15%.
The worry is what's next. Investors fear that artificial intelligence (AI) agents might take over tasks people now do with software like Adobe's, which bills subscribers per user, or seat.
If fewer people need a seat, Adobe's recurring revenue could shrink. That arguably makes this slump tougher to ride out than the past two. In 2002 and 2009, a sales recovery could show the hit was temporary. Now, Adobe needs to show that AI adds more to its business than it takes away.

It’s worth noting that we saw much the same situation with the recently announced Nike Alphafly 4. For that shoe, online commenters grumbled that it’s really just the Alphafly 3.1. Don't blame Intel's (INTC) weak guidance, tied to a prolonged memory chip supply shortage, for the fresh rout on tech stocks.
Blame the hyperscalers like Amazon (AMZN), Alphabet (GOOGL) and Meta (META) for not guiding Wall Street properly on how much they intended to spend this year and next on AI infrastructure. The bills are coming in much larger than expected, and Wall Street can't stomach it.
That's why you aren't seeing many heroes out there saying buy the dip right now. That's why Friday is shaping up to be another bloodbath for tech stocks.
Remember, it's cash flow that will be used to repay all the debt hyperscalers are poised to incur to support their robust AI infrastructure buildouts. The fact that cash flow is drying up because of a protracted period of spending is the bug causing the debt and stock markets to catch a cold.
Kudos to Amazon for at least not burying its free cash flow metric, the most important metric for tech at the moment, at the bottom of its earnings release. It made it no less tough to stomach, but at least it was easy to find quickly.
Amazon's free cash flow decreased to an outflow of $42.4 billion for the trailing twelve months, driven primarily by a year-over-year increase of $94.8 billion in purchases of property and equipment. This increase primarily reflects investments in artificial intelligence, Amazon said.
This compares to a free cash flow inflow of $14.8 billion for the trailing twelve months ended Sept. 30 of last year.
"We still expect 2026 cash capex of approximately $220 billion, the majority for AWS, and expect to spend meaningfully more in 2027," Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said on his earnings call.
Amazon's stock is down 7% in pre-market trading today.
On Wednesday evening, Google posted negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion in the quarter versus a Wall Street estimate for negative $3.5 billion.
Thursday saw more than $500 billion in market value wiped off Google.
Meta dropped a bombshell in its third quarter results last week, posting negative free cash flow for the first time since 2012. SpaceX (SPCX) burned about $9.9 billion in free cash flow in the quarter.
Both stocks have continued to sell off post earnings.
Hyperscaler free cash flow is likely to stay negative points out EvercoreISI strategist Julian Emanuel. The hyperscaler cohort of Meta, Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Oracle (ORCL) and SpaceX (SPCX) is now near a negative $200 billion expected over the next year Emanuel's research shows.

The decision by U.S. District Judge Richard Stearns in Boston grants a partial victory to the 25 Democratic-led states that sued the Trump administration in June, arguing that its new “medically frail” designation was too narrow and would make it too difficult for ill and disabled people to remain on Medicaid, the joint federal-state health insurance program for people with low incomes.
However, the decision also granted some concessions to the administration, most notably by allowing the new work requirements included in the measure known as the One Big Beautiful Big Act to remain in place.
Under that broad 2025 tax and spending law, states that have expanded Medicaid to cover more adults under the Affordable Care Act must require enrollees to work, go to school or volunteer for at least 80 hours a month.
In addition to the 40 states (plus the District of Columbia) that have expanded Medicaid under the ACA, the new rules will apply to Georgia, Tennessee and Wisconsin, which have used federal waivers to expand their Medicaid programs.

Judge rejects constitutional challenge to Missouri property tax caps tied to stadium bill
Cole County judge rules taxpayers, school districts and counties lack standing to sue, rejecting claims that the law unfairly treats different counties
Cole County Circuit Judge Christopher Limbaugh ruled that property tax caps included in a bill to support professional sports stadiums are constitutional(Anna Spoerre/Missouri Independent).
A Cole County judge on Wednesday rejected a constitutional challenge to property tax caps lawmakers added to a bill aimed at keeping the Kansas City Chiefs in Missouri.
The caps, structured as credits against property tax bills, applied to 97 of Missouri’s 114 counties. The caps, voted on in April, will mean this year’s property tax bill cannot be higher than last year in up to 22 counties, and cannot increase more than 5% in 75 others.
Of the 97 counties listed in the legislation, 61 passed it, 14 designated for tax bill freezes and 47 with the 5% cap; 12 counties rejected it; and 23 counties did not hold elections.
The law was challenged by two individuals, six school districts and one fire district. Forty-three counties, as well as individual county commissioners, later joined the case.
In his decision, Cole County Circuit Judge Christopher Limbaugh ruled that none of the plaintiffs had the right to sue and that they were wrong on the legal issues they raised.
Individuals do not have a right to sue simply because they believe they are at a disadvantage to a person in another county because of a property tax law, Limbaugh wrote. And the taxing districts can’t sue because they haven’t lost any money, he ruled.
The counties didn’t have the right to sue either, he wrote. They can’t raise issues on behalf of the school districts and other agencies they collect money for, he ruled.
“Missouri case law does not recognize standing based on dissatisfaction that other jurisdictions may impose different local taxes or conduct assessments differently; rather, Missouri case law recognizes standing where the plaintiff can show a present, direct adverse effect,” Limbaugh wrote.
The lawsuit was filed in September 2025, challenging the right of the legislature to write a law that provided property tax freezes in some counties, caps in others and no limits on increases in individual bills in 17 other counties and the city of St. Louis. The lawsuit alleged lawmakers used population and other characteristics to single out individual counties, creating special or local laws prohibited by the Missouri Constitution.
It was the second case challenging the stadium bill passed in a June 2025 special session. On Sept. 1, the Missouri Supreme Court heard an appeal in a separate lawsuit filed by two lawmakers and a conservative activist.
The court must decide whether state Sen. Mike Moon, an Ash Grove Republican, state Rep. Bryant Wolfin, a Ste. Genevieve Republican, and conservative activist Ron Calzone have standing. In January, Limbaugh ruled they did not and dismissed their lawsuit.
If the court finds Moon, Wolfin and Calzone do have standing, their case returns to Limbaugh.

I can’t help but notice, though: It looks like they just moved in. The kitchen as bare as a hotel kitchenette. A stack of cardboard boxes still unpacked. And an “art TV” presiding over the living room. The only reason I know it’s an art TV is because I have one, too. “The Frame,” by Samsung. A wall-mounted, bordered box designed to look like a painting or photograph, which you can choose from an extensive library, in lieu of the otherwise invasive screen it actually is. It was Conner’s Christmas gift to Kylie. Even though three years into their marriage, they have rarely, if ever, watched TV. “Which makes it kind of funny that we bought it!” says Kylie, scattering a bag of frozen broccoli florets onto a sheet pan. It’s also kind of funny, I think, that they have yet to select any art for the art TV, which renders it just an ordinary screen that’s seen neither Claude Monet nor the 2026 Winter Olympic Games, which at the time is well underway.
Maybe if it were the Summer Olympics?

State Treasurer Vivek Malek, pictured speaking in the Missouri State Capitol rotunda in 2025, shared the first annual performance report for the MOScholars voucher program Wednesday (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).
Missouri’s first report on the academic performance of students in its MOScholars voucher program found encouraging test scores but also exposed gaps in how the state collected the data, including information required by law that remains unavailable.
The report, released Wednesday by the Missouri Treasurer’s Office, found that students scored near the national average in reading and math during the program’s first three years. But researchers could validate test results for only 77% of students in testing grades, and the report lacked information about family income that state law requires.
The findings offer a baseline for measuring student performance but do not establish whether the program has improved academic outcomes or whether its students outperform those in public schools.
Researchers contracted to compile the report say they have an encouraging baseline to build on in future years. But the findings fall short of what some lawmakers expected from a program that has been operating for four years.
The law passed in 2021 that created the MOScholars program requires the state treasurer to “provide the test results and associated learning gains to the public via a state website after the third year of test and test-related data collection.”
Many expected this report last summer, immediately after the program’s third school year. When The Independent asked about the timing in April, the treasurer’s former chief of staff, Jackson Bailey, said the 2025-26 school year was “the fourth year of the MOScholars program, but is the third year of test and test-related data collection.” He said data for each school year is not collected until the following year.

Ahead of the Chicago Marathon, Clayton Young shared that he tore his hamstring, but still planned to compete. One of the strategies he said he used to get to the starting line and, ultimately, to the finish line as the first American: abandoning stretching in lieu of strength work—namely, isometric exercises.
When I heard this, I realized I had something in common with Young. My physical therapist, James Chung, PT, DPT, a sports performance physical therapist based in New York City, also recommends doing isometric strength exercises to deal with tendon issues, including my Achilles tendinopathy.
Isometrics are, indeed, great for pretty much everyone, says Mandy Fox, DPT, a physical therapist for runners in New York City. “An isometric exercise is a muscle contraction where the muscle produces force, but it doesn't change length and the joint angle doesn’t change,” Fox explains.
Basically, you’re loading the muscle and then holding it in one position for a set amount of time, like 30 seconds, as you would do in, say, a plank hold. This is in contrast to a concentric exercise, like lifting weights up to the top of a biceps curl, or an eccentric exercise, like slowly lowering heels down in a calf raise.
Whether you’re dealing with a hamstring tendon issue like Clayton, an Achilles tendon issue like me, or even a hip/glute tendon issue, this type of exercise can help. “This works because across the board, whether you’re elite or amateur, tendons respond to load, but they don’t respond to lengthening,” Fox says, adding that doing isometrics helps you keep running when you’re dealing with tendon issues.

For one, tendon pain is typically closer to where the joints are, says Chung, so you may feel Achilles tendon pain closer to the ankle and hamstring tendon issues at the sit bone or either side of the knee.
On the other hand, you’ll typically feel muscle strains or tears where the muscle contracts (and you feel pain when that happens). For example, with a calf strain, you might feel it most when you push off the ground, or with a hamstring strain, you might feel it most when your knee extends during the late swing phase of the gait cycle. You will also feel pain when you stretch a strained muscle.

On Sunday, November 1, nearly 60,000 runners taking on the New York City Marathon will get the rare privilege of having city traffic stop for them as they cover 26.2 miles through the five boroughs. This year also marks 50 years since the race moved beyond its original Central Park loops in 1976, expanding into the citywide event we know today.
There's a lot to keep up with, from the professional races and returning champions to a surprisingly large number of celebrities attempting 26.2 miles. And with coverage stretching from early morning into Sunday night, you don't necessarily have to be standing along First Avenue or waiting near Central Park to catch everyone in action.
Here's what you need to know about watching the race, including start times, broadcasts, and how to follow individual runners.
What Time Does the 2026 NYC Marathon Start?
Things get going at 8 a.m. ET with the men's professional wheelchair division, followed by the women's wheelchair racers at 8:02 a.m. Handcycles and select athletes with disabilities start at 8:22 a.m., before the professional women take off at 8:35 a.m. and the men follow at 9:05 a.m.
The rest of the field will leave Staten Island in five waves, beginning at 9:10 a.m. and continuing through 11:30 a.m.
How to Watch the 2026 NYC Marathon
The main national broadcast starts at 8 a.m. ET on ESPN2, with coverage running until 11:30 a.m. If you'd rather stream, the ESPN app has the same coverage with an ESPN Unlimited plan, plus an extra hour of prerace programming beginning at 7 a.m. and more action through 1 p.m. There's a Spanish-language feed during the main 8 to 11:30 a.m. window as well.
In New York and the surrounding tri-state area, ABC7/WABC-TV is another option. Coverage begins at 7 a.m., ahead of the race broadcast from 8 a.m. to 1 p.m., which you can also stream on the ABC 7 New York app.
For anyone more interested in the finish line than the rest of the course, ABC7NY.com and the ABC 7 New York app have you covered from 10:30 a.m. until 6 p.m. with a dedicated live stream. That should give you plenty of time to catch the professionals and stick around for the thousands of other runners making their way into Central Park.
ABC also has a national Live from the TCS New York City Marathon special scheduled for 3 to 5 p.m. Later that evening, NYRR is giving the final finishers their own broadcast from 8 to 10 p.m. on ABC7NY.com and its YouTube channel. The celebrations don't have to end just because the fastest runners finished hours earlier.
How to Track Runners
Planning to cheer for someone in Brooklyn and then catch them again in Manhattan? Before hopping on the subway, you'll probably want to check how far along they are, which is where the official New York Road Runners app comes in handy.
You can track individual runners throughout the race, check their progress at timing points, and pull up leaderboards and results. The app is available for iOS and Android, and it also has live feeds for each of the four professional races if you want to keep an eye on the elites while you're out cheering.
Who to Watch at the 2026 NYC Marathon
Last year's champions, Benson Kipruto and Hellen Obiri, are both coming back, and each has a memorable performance to defend. Kipruto won the closest men's finish in NYC Marathon history in 2025, while Obiri ran 2:19:51 to break the women's course record that had stood for 22 years.
Conner Mantz and Zouhair Talbi are among the Americans to watch in the men's race.

The selloff came after the company reported strong third-quarter results but issued a weaker-than-expected revenue forecast for the current quarter.
Reddit built much of its business around people discovering its discussions through Google searches, and those visitors are increasingly finding answers without ever clicking through to the platform. That puts pressure on the advertising business that has helped turn Reddit into one of the internet's fastest-growing publicly traded companies.
Reddit's third-quarter numbers initially looked healthy. Revenue climbed 53% year over year to $895 million, advertising revenue increased 54% to $847 million, and net income reached $283 million. CCH Connections 2026 main-stage panel explored agentic AI, talent development, trust, and the priorities firm leaders should set for the next year
ORLANDO, Fla., October 30, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Wolters Kluwer Tax & Accounting brought together leaders from Microsoft, Salesforce, McKinsey, and Sandra Wiley Strategies at CCH Connections 2026 with a clear message for accounting firms: as AI agents move from recommending actions to taking them, the time to decide how work gets done, how trust is earned, and how people build expertise is now. The main-stage panel, The New Blueprint: Building the Future-Ready Firm, moderated by Matt Linderman, Partner at McKinsey, drew on what each leader has learned from adopting and scaling AI.
On Wednesday, panelists urged firms not to wait for a perfect firmwide AI strategy. Start with one workflow, secure the data behind it, and build agentic workflows with the governance and controls to deliver the intended outcomes. The session closed with a challenge for every firm leader: set priorities for the next 12 months and choose one practical move to make in the next 90 days.
"The future-ready firm will not be defined by technology alone. It will be defined by how leaders combine technology with trusted expertise, sound judgment, strong relationships, and a clear understanding of the outcomes their clients need," said Jason Marx, CEO, Wolters Kluwer Tax & Accounting. "Bringing technology, business transformation, and firm leadership perspectives together helps professionals make informed decisions about where to act now and how to prepare for what comes next."
Key themes from the discussion:
-
AI is a business transformation opportunity, not simply a productivity tool. Panelists challenged firms to define the client outcomes and operating models they will need in the years ahead, then determine where AI can best enable them, instead of using the technology to simply automate today's processes.
-
Successful transformation requires changes in how firms develop people and organize work. As AI takes on more foundational tasks, firms need to consider how newer professionals will build expertise and judgment, and how training, supervision, team structures, and incentives should evolve.
-
Trust and governance will determine how far and how quickly AI can advance. As AI takes on more autonomous work, organizations need clear standards for evidence, accountability, and human oversight, including an understanding of when an AI agent should stop and defer to professional judgment. "Building an agent isn't the challenge. The challenge is integrating agents into business workflows with the right context, governance, and human judgment," said Lara Rubbelke, CTO and Vice President, Frontier Industry Advisory, Microsoft.
-
Firms should start small, measure results, and learn quickly. Value starts with deciding what outcome to drive, such as customer experience, employee productivity, or faster ROI. Anu Saha, SVP and COO, Agentforce, Salesforce urged firms to begin with one workflow and secure the data within it, noting that data transformation doesn't have to start with all of a firm's data at one time. Rather than waiting for every aspect of AI transformation to be resolved, panelists encouraged leaders to establish a small team, define how success will be measured, and use those lessons to guide where and how to scale.

Investors are getting nervous about AI infrastructure spending just as the Big Tech companies double down.
Over the past two weeks, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft have outlined plans to spend more than $740 billion on capital expenditures this year, which Wall Street is reading as AI infrastructure spending, including data centers and chips.
Earlier in the AI boom, investors largely rewarded such big outlays, viewing them as a sign of confidence in the technology's growth potential. But as we enter the fourth quarter, that enthusiasm seems to be giving way to concerns about negative free cash flow (spending more cash than a company brings in), mounting debt, and whether these enormous investments will ever generate enough returns.
The anxiety spilled across the market on Friday. The Nasdaq fell 2.9%, and chip stocks took a drubbing, too: Nvidia dropped 4%, Broadcom more than 5%, and Qualcomm 11%. Alphabet, which plummeted 12% on Thursday, its worst day on record, wiping out $500 billion in market value, fell again.

Google's parent company reported negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion in the third quarter, its second consecutive quarter in the red, even as quarterly capex grew to $51.4 billion. Alphabet expects to spend up to $205 billion this year, and expects that spending to keep rising in 2027.

The expanded global contact center partnership with Salesforce, together with a larger and longer dated credit line, indicates that management is positioning Bandwidth for higher cloud communications demand and potentially larger enterprise deal flow.
This article examines how Bandwidth's investment narrative is shaped by its record Q3 results and a deeper Salesforce tie up.
Scan how Bandwidth's latest quarter stacks up against peers by lining up its record revenue, fresh guidance and balance sheet firepower against 18 high quality undiscovered gems in similar niches.
Bandwidth Investment Narrative Recap
To own Bandwidth, you need to believe that cloud communications and AI driven voice use cases will keep pulling more large enterprises onto its platform, and that Maestro and deeper SaaS integrations can support that demand. The Q3 print, with higher sales and positive earnings, reinforces that the business can convert usage into profit, at least in the current setup.
The short term swing factor is whether Bandwidth can turn that record quarter and raised full year revenue guidance into sustained large deal momentum, especially as it leans into higher value AI and contact center workloads. The main risk is concentration and execution. A few large customers slowing usage, pricing pressure in CPaaS, or heavier R&D and network spend could quickly compress margins and make today's profitability less durable.
The most relevant fresh development is the fourth amendment to Bandwidth's Credit Agreement, which increases the revolving credit facility to US$200 million and pushes maturity out to October 26, 2031. For an investor, that extra liquidity and longer runway matter because this is a capital intensive platform that depends on ongoing investment in global network capacity and product.
That larger facility can support build out around Maestro, Salesforce integrations, and other enterprise wins without Bandwidth needing to lean immediately on equity markets. The flip side is higher reliance on external borrowing, which already flags as a risk, so you want to see management deploy that credit into projects that either deepen customer stickiness, reduce churn risk, or support higher margin AI and contact center traffic.
Analysts currently model Bandwidth reaching about US$1.1b in revenue and US$72.9m in earnings by 2029. This embeds an 11.2% annual revenue growth rate and an earnings increase of roughly US$70.6m from the US$2.3m level cited for earnings today.

Exploring Other Perspectives
Some of the most bullish analysts focus on Bandwidth's potential to push profit margins higher, not just revenue. Before this Q3 update, that group was already mapping out 14.5% annual top line growth and earnings of about US$144.0m by 2029. Those targets are far more optimistic than consensus, and this new Salesforce tie up and credit expansion could nudge forecasts again. You do not need to agree with either camp; however, it is worth comparing a few different narratives before you decide how Bandwidth fits in your portfolio.

Vulcan Materials NYSE: VMC said third-quarter adjusted EBITDA reached $707 million, with adjusted EBITDA margin expanding 20 basis points year over year to 32.3%, as higher selling prices and cost discipline helped offset substantial energy-related cost pressures.
Chief Executive Officer Ronnie Pruitt said the company’s underlying business adjusted EBITDA grew 5% during the quarter after accounting for roughly $40 million of energy cost headwinds and prior-year divestitures of more cyclical downstream businesses. The company now expects energy headwinds to exceed $100 million for the full year, with Chief Financial Officer Mary Andrews Carlisle later estimating the full-year impact could be about $120 million, including diesel and liquid asphalt costs.
Despite the demand environment remaining mixed, Pruitt said Vulcan expects to deliver approximately $2.4 billion in adjusted EBITDA for the year and another year of earnings growth.
Aggregates Pricing Offsets Higher Diesel Costs
Aggregates shipments declined 3% from a year earlier in the third quarter. Pruitt said the comparison was affected by favorable weather and unusually strong seasonally adjusted shipments in the prior-year period, following difficult winter weather and rainfall earlier that construction season.
On a seasonally adjusted basis, shipment momentum was similar to the second quarter and consistent with current market conditions, according to the company. Aggregates cash gross profit per ton rose modestly year over year as higher freight-adjusted selling prices more than offset sharply higher diesel costs.
Mix-adjusted average selling prices rose 5% from a year earlier, with improvement across geographies. Excluding diesel, aggregates freight-adjusted unit cash cost of sales increased 3%.
Pruitt said pricing remains Vulcan’s largest and fastest lever for managing inflation. The company sells about half of its products through daily bidding and about half through fixed-plant arrangements. Vulcan sent fixed-plant pricing announcements earlier this year to allow customers more time to prepare, he said.
For 2027, Vulcan expects aggregate prices to increase at a mid- to high-single-digit rate, including the effect of mix. The outlook reflects pricing actions taken this year, announced Jan. 1 increases and the company’s expectation that diesel costs will remain elevated. Pruitt said the company also expects to retain its discipline around midyear price increases.
“We will grow our cash gross profit per ton,” Pruitt said, noting that price increases are applied to a higher average selling price than cost increases are applied to on the company’s cost base.
Public Infrastructure, Large Projects Support Demand
Vulcan said public construction activity remains healthy, supported by remaining Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act funding. Pruitt said approximately 35% of IIJA funds have yet to be spent, while the current extension of federal highway authorization maintains funding at existing levels.

American sovereign debt surged during the week through Oct. 30, driven by a sharp pullback in tech shares linked to artificial intelligence and expanding corporate credit risk spreads that accelerated safe-haven flows into Treasuries.
Primary revenue channels for major American tech giants are demonstrating initial signs of cooling, even as total corporate artificial intelligence investments approach the $750 billion mark for the year. Intel (INTC) shares slipped on soft Q4 guidance, while Alphabet (GOOG, GOOGL) missed Q3 analyst expectations.
Meanwhile, costs to protect the debt of numerous U.S. technology heavyweights against default hit fresh record highs Friday. The protection price for Intel bonds for five years surged as much as 22.4 basis points Friday morning to 127.9 basis points a year, Bloomberg reported.
